1063-the-cask-of-amontillado:
Montresor, a proud Italian nobleman, lures his rival Fortunato, a wine connoisseur, into his damp vaults with the promise of a rare cask of Amontillado. Down the dark passages they go, past bones and nitre, until Montresor chains his guest and walls him in alive. Edgar Allan Poe tells the tale in a cool, vengeful voice.

No motive is ever fully given, which makes the horror colder: pride, insult, and a family motto do the work. The story runs only a few pages, yet its dread builds with each brick. It stands among Poe's most perfect tales of revenge, and it is often a reader's first taste of his art.
12298-the-grand-can-on-of-the-colorado:
John Muir published The Grand Canyon of the Colorado in 1902, a short book praising the canyon as earth greatest wonder. Muir, the Scottish-American naturalist who helped create the national parks, writes with prophetic fire.

The book opens by mocking the modern tourist, padded with plush, graded roads, tunnels, and steam, eager to see all kingdoms of the world without effort. Muir answers with the canyon itself: alabaster fountains pouring life-giving floods, gulches given passionate torrents, and lightning answered by roaring water. The prose urges readers to meet wildness on foot, not through glass. The book is a founding text of American conservation.
12655-the-boy-mechanic-volume-1-700-thin:
The Boy Mechanic, volume one, August 1916, offers seven hundred things for boys to do, with eight hundred illustrations. A presentation note from Mother, dated January 1938, fronts a text that reproduces the original except for Gutenberg layout rules, with each project followed by its page number for the index.

Projects range from magic, kites and boomerangs to chemical photography, phonographs and other historical crafts. The transcriber warns that the text-only version is limited, since diagrams matter, and urges the PDF for full use. The volume captures early twentieth-century boy culture: make, mend and invent, with tools, patience and daring.
15160-on-commando:
Dietlof van Warmelo's 1902 memoir tells of Boer commando life in the South African war, with a portrait frontispiece and a foreword from Holland. Chapters follow the entry into Natal, the siege of Ladysmith, the Tugela battles, and guerrilla life on the Magalies Mountains. Narrow escapes for Presidents Steyn and De Wet feature.

Van Warmelo writes as a participant, with practical hints, treks, and battles from Nooitgedacht to Boesmanskop. His account favors the Boer side, which makes it a partisan source, not a neutral history. War readers will find it vivid, detailed, and valuable as a voice from inside the commando.
1658-phaedo:
Friends gathered in a prison cell to watch Socrates die, and one of them, Phaedo, later told the story to listeners at Phlius who had not been there. Friends gather around the condemned man, who talks calmly, bathes, and takes the hemlock while they weep.

Most of the dialogue is Socrates' argument that the soul does not die with the body, built on ideas about opposites, recollection, and the soul's kinship with what is unseen. It is both a death scene and a work of philosophy. Readers come away with a vivid picture of Socrates as his friends remembered him: steady, questioning, and unafraid.
23142-in-search-of-el-dorado:
Two adventurers trade the sea for the jungle in In Search of El Dorado. Chance threw the two men together and proved their mettle. After that the sea lost them. Swamps and forests of the Amazon Valley claimed them instead, with amazing adventures ahead. Dick Cavendish had shipped as fifth officer of the Everest.

El Dorado, the golden kingdom that swallowed expeditions whole, draws Dick and his companion upriver in Harry Collingwood's credited adventure. Piranha water, lost trails, and hostile country replace the quarterdeck's order. Boys' imperial fiction ran on such substitutions, salt water for black water. The Amazon chapters keep the pace of the sea chapters, with greener dangers and the same stout hearts.
23541-dick-marjorie-and-fidge-a-search-f:
G. E. Farrow, author of Adventures in Wallypug Land, wrote this search for the wonderful dodo, with many pictures by Allan Wright. Dick, Marjorie, and Fidge set out to find a bird most folk deem lost, and a skipper finds the poor creature looking the picture of misery, asking if he feels better.

Farrow dedicates the book to his dear little friends, thanking boys and girls of all ages and sizes, from all parts of the world, for kind letters on his earlier books. The quest moves through strange lands and comic scrapes, with the dodo as both prize and joke. Children will enjoy the hunt, the heroes' pluck, and the dodo's sad, funny face, in a tale that treats a lost bird as a grand adventure.
24342-the-story-of-the-outlaw-a-study-of:
Emerson Hough wrote this study of the western desperado, published by the Outing Publishing Company in New York in 1907. Its subtitle promises historical narratives of famous outlaws, stories of noted border wars, vigilante movements, and armed conflicts on the frontier. The frontispiece shows Plummer's men holding up the Bannack stage, from a painting by John W. Norton.

Chapters run from the desperado, the imitation desperado, the land of the desperado, and the early outlaw. Vigilantes of California, the outlaw of the mountains, Henry Plummer, and Boone Helm follow. Death scenes of desperadoes come next, with Joseph A. Slade. The desperado of the plains and Wild Bill Hickok lead to frontier wars, the Lincoln County War, and the Stevens County War. Biographies of bad men, and bad men of Texas and the Indian nations, close the book. Readers get a full gallery of frontier violence.
24436-anything-you-can-do:
Darrel T. Langart wrote this science fiction novel, published by Doubleday and Company in Garden City, New York, in 1963. It is a first edition copyrighted in 1963, with a shorter version earlier in Analog Science Fact and Science Fiction. Its dedication runs, for mon cher ami Frère Gascé, a man I may truly call my brother. The novel opens like a great silver-pink fish singing through the eternal night.

The fish shape has neither fins nor tail, hovering as if in wait for a smaller species to swoop down out of nowhere, so it in turn could pounce and kill. Yet still it moves and sings, and only a being familiar with the type could tell that this particular fish is dying. In shape the ship is rather like a narrow flounder, long and tapered, oval in cross-section. Readers get a dying ship, singing through night.
28401-free-and-impartial-thoughts-on-the:
Free and Impartial Thoughts on the Sovereignty of God, second edition, London, 1745, argues against election, reprobation, and original sin. The anonymous author, addressing all who profess those doctrines, says Christianity was given for human benefit, yet Christians differ greatly on what genuine Christianity is. J. Robinson printed the book at the Golden Lion in Ludgate Street.

The writer holds that a perfect God would give clear rules, as good men and states give clear laws, and that obscure passages cannot be a fit rule of faith. His tone is earnest and rational, seeking better helps for inquiry. The pamphlet offers an early, plain-spoken case for free and impartial thought.
29141-two-new-pocket-gophers-from-wyomin:
E. Raymond Hall and H. Gordon Montague wrote this 1951 paper, Two New Pocket Gophers from Wyoming and Colorado, in the University of Kansas natural history series. Montague studied how Thomomys talpoides of Wyoming varies by place in 1947 to 1948, using museum material, but release waited until Colorado samples from near areas could be checked. In autumn 1950, Hall checked the Colorado samples and new Wyoming material from two seasons of field work.

The studies name two new kinds of the northern pocket gopher in southeast Wyoming. The authors thank the Biological Surveys collection of the United States National Museum for the Colorado samples. Readers get a short, exact piece of mammal naming work, showing how patient museum study names new forms.
30742-anything-you-can-do:
Darrell T. Langart writes Anything You Can Do, an illustrated, shorter version of a longer work, first of two parts, from Analog, May and June 1962, illustrated by Leone. Its premise states the alien was really alien, Earth faced a strange problem, a superman was needed, and there were none.

The story opens with a ship like a great silver-pink fish singing through eternal night. It has no fins or tail, and hovers as if waiting for smaller prey to swoop down so it could pounce and kill. Still it moves, though only a being who watches closely could tell how. Langart builds a first-contact tale around Earth's search for a hero it does not have.
31035-mammals-of-mesa-verde-national-par:
Sydney Anderson's 1961 report surveys the mammals of Mesa Verde National Park in Colorado, published as volume 14, number 3 of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series. Field work began with a family vacation in August and early September 1956, when Anderson and his wife Justine collected and studied animals in the park, with later help from collector J. R. Alcorn and Colorado game biologists.

The report sets the animals against the park's geology, the northern edge of a Cretaceous sandstone deposit called the Mesaverde group, and records species, ranges, and habits across its mesas and canyons. It serves both as a baseline for later park wildlife work and as a readable account of what lives in a rugged corner of the Southwest.
31148-a-new-subspecies-of-wood-rat-neoto:
Robert B. Finley Jr.'s 1953 paper names a new wood rat subspecies, Neotoma mexicana scopulorum, from eastern Colorado south of the Arkansas River. Field and museum studies showed the new form most distinctive near Two Buttes and Higbee, where it differs in skull characters from its neighbors fallax and inopinata and averages slightly larger. Its fur color cannot be told apart.

The type, an old adult male trapped three miles northwest of Higbee at 4,300 feet in May 1950, anchors the description. The range runs through canyons, mesas, and foothills east to Two Buttes and south to Clayton, New Mexico. Published as volume 5, number 30 of the Kansas museum series, it is the formal record for this Colorado wood rat.
31280-mammals-of-the-grand-mesa-colorado:
Sydney Anderson's 1959 paper, volume 9, number 16 of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series, reports the mammals of Colorado's Grand Mesa. The mesa, a westward extension of the central Colorado mountains, stands more than five thousand feet above the Colorado and Gunnison valleys. It forms a peninsula of cool, moist forest ringed by hot, dry, barren lowland.

Warren's 1942 Mammals of Colorado had mentioned only four species from the mesa's counties. Anderson records twenty-two species from the mesa and two localities below its north rim on preserved specimens, plus five more by observation, extending some subspecies' ranges westward. Specimens came from a 1954 field party led by Harrison B. Tordoff, with later material from Phillip M. Youngman. The paper remains the baseline fauna of a high island in the Rockies.
33653-a-new-pocket-gopher-genus-thomomys:
E. Raymond Hall describes a previously unnamed subspecies of pocket gopher from Wyoming and Colorado in this short 1951 paper from the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History. Among abundant specimens of the widespread Thomomys talpoides from Wyoming, those from the Sierra Madre range proved on comparison to belong to a distinct form, which Hall names Thomomys talpoides meritus.

The type is an adult male, skull and skin, taken at 8,800 feet in Carbon County, Wyoming, in July 1948. Its range covers the Sierra Madre range of southern Wyoming and northern Colorado, and its diagnosis notes small size and dark coloration. The four-page paper is a compact example of mammal taxonomy built on museum specimens and careful geographic comparison.
34836-a-new-pocket-gopher-genus-thomomys:
A New Pocket Gopher From Eastern Colorado, by Raymond Hall, is a short paper in animal naming. It ran in the University of Kansas Publications of the Museum of Natural History in October 1951. The paper fills pages 81 to 85 of its volume.

Hall treats the pocket gophers of east-central Colorado, long put under one Wyoming subspecies. Two new races named in 1951 along the state line now cut those animals off from their old kin. That leaves the Colorado stock in doubt, and Hall tests old names against the specimens at hand. Neither of the old names fits, his study finds. The paper sets out the traits that mark the stock as its own form. Such papers fix the map of where each race of beast lives.
36577-a-claim-on-klondyke-a-romance-of-t:
A Claim on Klondyke is a romance of the gold rush by Edward Roper. Blackwood published it at Edinburgh and London in 1899. Roper had written By Track and Trail through Canada. The preamble opens near midnight in January 1897. A man muffled in furs stands on glittering snow among low hills. A great long haired dog stands listening beside him. The cold is so intense that any wind would kill a man standing still.

Moonlight and stars make the scene bright enough to read by. Illustrations show Myles Canyon, the Five Fingers Rapids, and Lake La Barge. The Yukon at the mouth of the Klondyke River appears too. A dug out, a tunnel, and a sluice picture the claim itself. The subtitle calls the Klondike the Arctic El Dorado. Adventure in the frozen north drives the tale.
37492-the-chalice-of-courage-a-romance-o:
The Chalice of Courage, a romance of Colorado, is a novel by Cyrus Townsend Brady, printed at New York in 1912. Harrison Fisher and J N Marchand drew the illustrations. Brady dedicates the book to his beloved friend John B Walker, Junior, a great-hearted man of Colorado. The novel is built in five books.

The first, The Higher Law, opens with the cup that would not pass, and a figure alone upon the trail. The second book, The East and the West, brings the young lady from Philadelphia. The pool and the water sprite, the bear, the man, and the flood fill its chapters. The third book tells of forgetfulness: a wild dash for the hills, the log hut in the mountains, and the castaways of the mountains. Later books are named for the woman's heart and the man's heart.
37918-rocky-mountain-national-park-color:
Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado, is a government guide booklet printed at Washington in 1937. It bears the names of the Secretary of the Interior, Harold Ickes, and of the National Park Service director, Arno Cammerer. An opening feature asks, do you know your national parks, and runs a roll of the system.

Acadia joins mountain and seacoast, Glacier holds two hundred lakes and sixty glaciers, and the Grand Canyon is called the world's greatest example of erosion. The home entry gives Rocky Mountain peaks from 11,000 to 14,255 feet in the heart of the Rockies. The park was established in 1915 and covers a little over four hundred square miles, the largest single entry in this roll after the Alaskan giant.
38690-what-shall-we-do:
What Shall We Do holds essays of faith and life by Leo Tolstoy. A free press in London spread his works in cheap form in those years. The front page states the press creed in bold plain words. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

The creed holds that mans true aim is unity in reason and love. It calls men brethren and bids each rout false aims from his own self. False wants in creed, trade, and rule are blamed for most of mans pain. Tolstoy is named the great voice of that faith in the age. The essays press his call to plain life and love of all men.
40762-dodo-s-daughter-a-sequel-to-dodo:
A society novel by E F Benson, published at New York in 1914. The Century Company held the 1913 copyright. The book continues Benson's famous Dodo books. Dodo herself is now a mother in North Wales. Her daughter Nadine holds the stage here. The family cottage at Meering squeezes in eighteen guests.

Nadine has claimed the old smoking-room as her bedroom. Everyone now smokes everywhere, she argues, so the room is free. She paints it entirely black, carpet, walls, and ceiling. Against black, her friends look like gems, she explains. Mud on snow was their effect against white. Visitors drift in after official bedtime for more talk. Benson writes the clan's sparkle with amused precision.
41950-the-visions-of-quevedo:
The Visions of Quevedo holds dream satires by the great Spanish wit in English. William Elliot turned the Spanish text for this American print. The book came out at Philadelphia in the year eighteen thirty two. The front note claims this was the sole English turn of the work then.

Dream trips through hell and the world show knaves of each trade in turn. French turns of the work ran to five in past years, the note says. Sharp blame of fools, priests, and proud men fills the famed dreams. Brief scenes and tart talk mark the wit of Spains keen age. The work stands as a chief fruit of that lands great prose age.
44585-the-boy-mechanic-book-2-1000-thing:
The Boy Mechanic, book 2, subtitled 1000 Things for Boys to Do, was copyrighted in 1915 by Windsor and published in Chicago by the Popular Mechanics company, with 995 pictures. The cover promises devices for winter sports, a motion-picture camera, indoor games, reed furniture, electrical novelties, boats, fishing rods, camps, kites and gliders, pushmobiles, a roller coaster, and a Ferris wheel.

An early article teaches plane-table surveying with tools a boy can make at home. Surveying and map making, the piece argues, are among the most absorbing parts of an engineer's work, and Washington himself learned the trade young. Projects give full directions and lists of materials, sized for a home workshop and a boy's pocket money.
45608-mr-dide-his-vacation-in-colorado:
Mr Dide, His Vacation in Colorado is a sport and travel book by France, author of past works on the rod and line and on the trails and parks of that state. It was set in type by a state press in the mid west and held in law in the year cut on its title page.

Its parts read like a camp log in tale form. A cold slot and a warm trail open the trip, then twin lakes high in the hills. A pass through a great range, a man named for a prophet of old, and runs on two wild rivers fill the mid book. Sport, luck and its lack, thin air, and a famed peak close the jaunt. A word first sings the call of the wilds for the man who seeks them with love.
47760-three-hundred-things-a-bright-boy-:
Three Hundred Things a Bright Boy Can Do is a handbook of sports, crafts, and pastimes, written by many hands. It was published in London by Sampson Low in 1914, and is fully illustrated. The title is the programme: three hundred ways for a boy to fill his hours.

The chapters begin with the body. Training, gymnastics, walking, running, and jumping come first. Hockey, Indian clubs, swimming, rowing, and boxing follow. The ice, the river, and the camp kitchen each get a chapter. Then the book turns quiet. Butterflies and moths, aquariums, and the garden occupy the middle pages. The boy as artist takes up a long stretch. Talking through the belly, stage magic, and pets come near the end. Things boys can make and fireside amusements close the set.
53251-the-lusitania-s-last-voyage-being-:
Lusitania Last Voyage is a survivor narrative by Charles Lauriat the younger. Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York issued it in October nineteen fifteen. Lauriat was one of the survivors of the torpedoed liner that May. A photo of the Lusitania under steam fronts the sad account here.

The ship was sunk by a German submarine off the Irish coast. The date was May seventh nineteen fifteen, in the second year of war. Lauriat gives the book to his father, who taught him to swim in boyhood. His mother faith, he says, has brought him through all things since. A poem, The Zone, opens the narrative with a plea for pity.
56588-new-ideas-for-work-and-play-what-a:
New Ideas for Work and Play: What a Girl Can Make and Do is an activity book for girls, packed with illustrations. The transcriber's note counts numbered figures past five hundred, which shows the scale of the picture matter. Every project in such a book hangs on its drawings, and here they crowd the text.

The title states the plan in full. Work and play are joined: things to make and things to do, gathered as new ideas for a girl's hands and hours. The many illustrations appear within the text at the point where each is needed. Three figures stand out of order in the original printing, a quirk the editors kept while noting that all references to them are correct. The book belongs to the age when a thick, cheerful manual of crafts and pastimes was a standard gift for a young reader.
60131-estes-park-colorado:
Estes Park, Colorado is a booster booklet for the town at the east gate of Rocky Mountain National Park. The town stands at seven thousand five hundred and forty-nine feet. The booklet calls the park the nation's greatest playground and the town its centre.

Pages list daily mail, telegraph and phone links, a public library, churches, and a weekly paper. An aviation club offers a three-thousand-foot runway, golf, tennis, and scenic flights. Shops, the booklet says, supply every need, with daily delivery to outlying districts. Nearby stands the head office of the Colorado-Big Thompson project. Its thirteen-mile tunnel will carry river water through the Rockies.
60143-prairie-peak-and-plateau-a-guide-t:
Prairie, Peak and Plateau is a guide to the rocks and landforms of Colorado by John and Halka Chronic. It is bulletin 32 of the Colorado Geological Survey, issued in 1972 and sold for two dollars. The front matter sets out the survey's charges from the state.

The survey was set up again in February 1969. Its tasks are to advise state and town bodies on rock and ground problems. It must push the winning of minerals, list the state's stores of ore, and mark places of hazard. The book puts that knowledge into a guide for the lay reader. Prairie, peak, and plateau are the three great faces of Colorado. The guide reads each one in turn as the work of deep time.
6090-what-can-she-do:
E. P. Roe dedicates What Can She Do, in spirit, to girls who refuse to play Micawber, waiting for someone to turn up and carry their helpless weight. His preface says the book was not written to amuse or win praise as art, but with a definite, earnest purpose.

As society grows older and leaves primitive simplicity, many grow rich while more grow poor, and the ordinary avenues of industry grow thronged. Roe warns of the fearful risk for a woman thrown on the world with unskilled hands, untrained mind, and unbraced moral nature. The novel urges training and self-reliance.
63859-my-wayward-pardner-or-my-trials-wi:
Marietta Holley's My Wayward Pardner; or, My Trials with Josiah, America, the Widow Bump, and Etcetery was published by subscription only, at Hartford, Connecticut, in 1882, under a copyright of 1880. Holley writes as Josiah Allen's Wife, the name she had made with My Opinions and Betsey Bobbet's and Samantha at the Centennial. True Williams drew the pictures, and the book is given to Josiah and America themselves.

The preface is a set-to with Josiah. Her mind, she tells him, has been dreadfully agitated over that lot of women who suffer more than tongue can tell, and she means to write about them. Josiah counsels letting them write it themselves. Her answer begins with the day he fell through the barn and broke his limb.
64012-puck-s-broom-the-wonderful-adventu:
E Gordon Browne wrote Puck’s Broom, the gay adventures of George Henry and his dog. Kathleen I Nixon drew the plates for the tale of faery. Moffat, Yard and Company issued it in New York in nineteen hundred twenty three. Puck sweeps the dust behind the door, his old rhyme says.

George Henry scorns the fairies, to their great hurt pride. His birthday tea brings games, fireworks, and one shock more. A fairy bid to their woodland party finds him on Midsummer Eve. Dream music calls the sick boy in his cross ill days. A small green gate leads him and Alexander to the Land of Dreams. Father Time sits by the sea with his glass in that far land. Wish hard, the rule runs there, and doors of dreams swing wide. Puck in the end stands close, broom in hand, through all the fun.
64349-in-quest-of-el-dorado:
In Quest of El Dorado is a travel book by Stephen Graham, issued at New York in 1923. Graham dedicates it to the literary memory of a friend shot by accident at Mexico City on the last night of 1922. The contents set out a long arc of travel in five books. It opens in Spain, at Madrid, and goes on toward Cadiz.

The second book, The Indies, follows the Columbus journey to Porto Rico, Santo Domingo, and Cuba. A third book turns to New Mexico, with cowboys, Indians, and local Mexicans in chapters of their own. Panama follows, with a climb in Darien and an account of the canal. A final book takes up two old golden quests of the Spanish age, then returns to New York. The route itself retells the search the title names.
64722-alpha-say-beta-do:
Alpha Say, Beta Do is a tale by Alfred Maxwell from Planet Stories magazine. The tale ran in the Summer 1950 issue of that pulp sheet. Doyle Tindar and Kay Kanton had themselves duplicated for space trouble work. Duplication stood as standard practice for trouble-shooters in that future world. But the duplicates fell in love, which was neither practice nor standard.

Doyle Tindar wakes to the buzzing visor-phone beside his bed one morning. Sam Penset of the Control Board shows his fat, grim face on it. No reports came from the mines on Bolus the night before, he booms. Radio contact stands dead, and the power plant may have caught a meteor. Tindar protests that he is on his first vacation in a year. Bedding is on honeymoon and Teppen is getting new teeth planted. Kay Kanton, a meter-reader, cannot report fully on the mines there.
6610-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
Skinner's fifth volume heads south, to lights and shadows from Maryland to the Gulf. A swim at Indian Head opens the set. Great guns now boom there on proving grounds. Later tales run through the Dismal Swamp, the Natural Bridge, Toccoa Falls, and the sacred fire of Natchez. Ghosts, sirens, and avengers haunt these warm, wet lands.

Each tale is short, with a place at its core and a moral or a shiver at its close. The south here is lush and strange, full of rivers, swamps, and old wars. Lights and Shadows of the South gives southern lore the same brisk, neighborly telling Skinner gave the Hudson.
66507-cholera-and-the-water-supply-in-th:
John Snow wrote Cholera and the Water Supply in the South Districts of London in 1854, reprinted from the Journal of Public Health for October 1856. Snow first set out his views on cholera in the summer of 1849. A brief sketch of those views opens the paper. Snow holds that cholera starts in the gut, not in the blood.

No proof shows blood poison at the start, Snow says. Proof shows the ill can pass from man to man, he holds. The stuff that causes the ill must reach the gut and grow there, he argues. It then passes off to cause fresh cases. Crowded poor homes where folk eat, drink, cook, and sleep in one room spread it fast. Soiled linen and hands carry it to food, he warns.
8082-canyons-of-the-colorado:
John Wesley Powell, former director of the United States Geological Survey, wrote this account of the canyons of the Colorado, first published in 1895, with many illustrations. His preface recalls returning from the first exploration to find newspapers reporting disaster, with obituaries circulating for a party believed lost save one man. Powell, amused to read his own high reputation in those notices, set out to tell the true story of the river journey.

The book describes the 1869 expedition down the Green and Colorado rivers through canyons no one had mapped, with boats, rapids, and dwindling supplies. It combines adventure with geology, as Powell reads the rock walls for Earth's history. It remains a classic of American exploration, and the founding text of Grand Canyon literature.
8670-in-the-heart-of-the-rockies-a-story:
G. A. Henty sets this boys' adventure in Colorado, where Tom's choice launches a journey across plains, rivers, and mountains. Early chapters find friends, cross the plains, and meet Leaping Horse, before danger, chases, an avalanche, and a hard winter test the party. A hunting dog saving Jerry from rapids, shooting lessons, and a snow fort all feature among the illustrated episodes.

Later the boys travel by canoe down the Colorado, reach the Grand Canyon, and return to Denver, with a fortune waiting at the end of the trail. An Indian attack and a fresh start keep the pace brisk. Henty's formula, decent lads, loyal friends, and danger met head-on, is on full display. Young readers get a rattling Western, and older ones a clear sample of how Victorian boys' books pictured the American frontier.
britannica-1911-accolti-bernardo:
Bernardo Accolti (1465-1536) was an Italian poet born at Arezzo, son of Benedetto Accolti, the jurist and historian. His own age knew him as l'Unico Aretino, the unique man of Arezzo, for his fame as a reciter of impromptu verse. Crowds of learned men and distinguished prelates gathered to hear him invent on the spot, and Cardinal Bembo left testimony to his extraordinary talent.

Print was less kind. The poems Bernardo published at Florence in 1513, under titles including Virginia and Strambotti, show brilliant fancy but scarcely justify his reputation. The entry judges that he likely succeeded better in performances made on the moment than in work produced by deliberation.
britannica-1911-agostini-leonardo:
Leonardo Agostini was an Italian student of old art and coins. He lived and worked in the 1600s. He was born at Siena. His first work was to gather works of art. He did that work for the Barberini palace in Rome. The pope of the day then gave him a new post. He was put in charge of old remains for the Roman states. His books made his name more widely known.

Two works carry his name to this day. He brought out a new set of Paruta's Sicilian Medals. Four hundred more coins were cut in plates for it. With Giovanni Bellori he wrote on carved gems of old date. That book was put into Latin by Jakob Gronovius. It came out at Amsterdam in 1685. Agostini shows the learned taste of Rome in his age. Popes and great homes prized old things as marks of rank.
britannica-1911-albinovanus-pedo:
Almost nothing survives of Albinovanus Pedo, a Roman poet of the Augustan age, yet three great names vouch for him. Ovid, his close friend, names Pedo's Theseis, an epic on Theseus, in a letter. Martial praises his epigrams. Quintilian gives him measured praise as an epic poet. Pedo also wrote an epic on the deeds of Germanicus and won fame as a fine teller of tales.

One lovely piece remains, kept by the speaker Seneca. It tells of Germanicus's voyage in A.D. 16 down the river Ems to the Northern Ocean, caught by the storm Tacitus also tells of. Three elegies long set down to Pedo by Scaliger are now held by most judges not to be his at all. One of them is a comfort piece for Livia on the death of Drusus.
britannica-1911-aleardi-aleardo:
Aleardi, Aleardo, Count Aleardi, an Italian poet of 1812 to 1878, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Verona in November 1812, he became an Austrian subject soon after birth, since Verona then lay under Austria. He was inspired from his cradle, the entry says, with hatred of the foreigner. That feeling barred him from the public service his rank entitled him to, and his patriotic verses could not be published.

A narrative poem, Arnaldo da Rocca, still appeared in 1842, and the revolutionary year 1848 opened the way for his Lettere a Maria. He joined the popular uprising and was imprisoned for a time. His finest piece, an ode to Italy's maritime cities, came in 1856. After Austria's expulsion from Lombardy he returned to Verona, issued his poems collected in 1862, and became professor, deputy, and finally senator. The entry judges that his patriotic warmth outran his poetry, though he excelled in description.
britannica-1911-bartolommei-marquis-ferd:
Marquis Ferdinando Bartolommei (1821–1869), an Italian revolutionary and statesman from an old noble Florentine family, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Though aristocratic by birth, his sympathies lay with the democratic party. In 1847–1848 his house served as a centre for revolutionary committees in Tuscany. After the grand duke returned under Austrian protection in 1849, Bartolommei was confined to his estate and then exiled for a year for spreading seditious writings.

Conspiracy at home fills the next decade. Back in Florence from 1853, Bartolommei kept a secret printing press in his palace. He worked with Cavour's Piedmontese liberals, organized Tuscan volunteers for war against Austria, and spent his own money freely. In April 1859 Florence rose, the troops refused to fire, and the grand duke left for good. Bartolommei became gonfaloniere of the provisional government, backed union with Italy under Victor Emmanuel, and sat as a senator.
britannica-1911-bastinado:
Bastinado, named from the Spanish baston and French bâton, a stick or cudgel, is a punishment described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was the European name for a form of punishment common in the East, especially in Turkey, Persia, and China. The blows fell with a light stick or bamboo lath on the soles of the feet or the buttocks. The victim was held down while the beating went on.

Fear of the bastinado lay in duration, not force. The entry stresses that the blows themselves were scarcely more than tapping, light strokes rather than heavy strikes meant to break skin or bone at once. What made the punishment a terror was its long continuation, stroke after stroke with no quick end in sight. A skilful bastinadoist, a man practised in giving the punishment, could kill his victim after hours of such torture, the entry concludes.
britannica-1911-bentivoglio-guido:
Guido Bentivoglio (1579–1644) was an Italian cardinal, statesman and historian born at Ferrara. After study at Padua he settled at Rome, where Pope Clement VIII favoured him and made him private chamberlain. Paul V raised him to archbishop of Rhodes in 1607 and sent him as nuncio to Flanders and then to France.

Back at Rome in 1621 Bentivoglio became cardinal and managed French affairs at the papal court for Louis XIII. Close to Pope Urban VIII, he was tipped to succeed him, but died suddenly as the conclave opened in September 1644. His works include a history of the war in Flanders, reports from his two nuncio posts, and diplomatic letters long read as classics in Italian schools.
britannica-1911-boulder-colorado:
Boulder is a city in Colorado at the foot of the mountains, county seat of Boulder county, about 30 miles north-west of Denver. It stands about 5300 feet above the sea on Middle Boulder Creek. Its people grew from 3330 in 1890 to 6150 in 1900 and 9539 in 1910. Three railways served it, one climbing to the mining camps with fine mountain views.

The state university of Colorado, chartered in 1861 and opened in 1877, is the town's pride. It holds colleges of arts, medicine, law, engineering, commerce, and education, and a library of some 42,000 volumes. A city park of 2840 acres and three fine canyons lie close by. At the south edge, 400 feet above the town, sits the Colorado Chautauqua summer school. The climate is praised for chest complaints.
britannica-1911-bruni-leonardo:
Leonardo Bruni (1369–1444) was an Italian scholar, author of the History of Florence, born at Arezzo and generally known as Leonardo Aretino. He served as secretary to the papal chancery under Innocent VII and John XXII. From 1427 until his death in 1444 he was chancellor to the republic of Florence, a civic career the short entry sets out plainly.

Florence buried him at state expense in Santa Croce, where his laurelled statue can still be seen. He was the first writer to free the history of Florence from its fabulous elements, clearing myth out of the city's past, though the entry judges his book. Not unintelligent, one that only repays very laborious study. Its Latin edition of twelve books, a Tuscan translation by Donato Acciajuoli printed at Venice in 1476, and later reprints with Sansovino's continuation are listed for readers.
britannica-1911-carbonado:
Carbonado is a dark, impure form of diamond. In Brazil it is also called “carbonate,” and in trade just carbon. This 1911 Britannica article describes the stone. It is sometimes called black diamond as well. It occurs in small masses of irregular many-sided form. The colour runs black, brown or dark grey. Its lustre is dull and resin-like to the eye. Its fracture is granular and paler than the surface.

Carbonado is slightly cellular in structure. So its specific gravity is below that of crystallized diamond. It is found almost only in Bahia, in Brazil. There it lies in the cascalho, the diamond gravel. Borneo yields a small quantity of it too. The stone was once thought nearly worthless. Diamond drills changed that view completely. Leschot's drills used its hardness for boring rock. The article gives its place in that trade.
britannica-1911-castello-bernardo: Genoese painter Bernardo Castello, born in fifteen fifty seven, is the subject of a brief 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. He painted portraits and history scenes. He was a close friend of the poet Tasso. He took on the task of designing the figures for Tasso's epic poem. That work was published in fifteen ninety two, and some designs were engraved by Agostino Carracci. Castello painted many works in Genoa, most in a fast and light style. He also worked in Rome and at the Savoy court.
britannica-1911-cavalcanti-guido:
Guido Cavalcanti (c. 1250–1300) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Italian poet and philosopher. His father was a philosopher whom Dante places among the Epicureans and Atheists in the Inferno. Guido himself was Dante's friend. By his marriage to Beatrice, daughter of Farinata Uberti, he became head of the Ghibellines. When Florence tired of party brawls, it banished the leaders of both sides.

Cavalcanti was sent to Sarzana. There he caught a fever, and he died of it. He left love sonnets and canzoni that Dante praised. Some are simple and graceful. Many, the entry says, are spoiled by metaphysics drawn from Plato, Aristotle, and the Christian Fathers. Most honour a French lady he calls Mandetta. His Canzone d'Amore was very popular and often published. His complete poems appear in Giunti's collection of 1527. He also wrote prose on philosophy and oratory.
britannica-1911-cicognara-leopoldo:
Cicognara, Leopoldo, Count (1767–1834) was an Italian archaeologist and writer on art, born at Ferrara on 17 November 1767. Science tempted him a while, but residence at Rome, given to painting and to the antiquities and galleries there, fixed his bent. Travel through Naples, Sicily, Florence, Milan, Bologna and Venice gave him a complete knowledge of their art. From 1795 he spent twelve years in politics at Modena.

In 1808 he became president of the Academy of the Fine Arts at Venice, raising professor numbers, improving courses, founding prizes and starting a gallery for Venetian pictures. His Storia della scultura, issued from 1813 to 1818 with 180 plates, aimed to complete the works of Winckelmann and D'Agincourt. Splendid publishing ventures left him poor, and his library of thirty years was sold to Pope Leo XII in 1824 for the Vatican. He died on 5 March 1834.
britannica-1911-commando: Commando is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica entry on a Boer force term from South Africa. The word is Portuguese for command in its root sense. The Boers took it up, and English use came through them. It named army raids against native peoples. More than that, a commando was the base unit of the old Boer republics. Law there made army service a duty for all males. The age span ran from sixteen years to sixty. Each commando was raised from the men of one voting district.
britannica-1911-demetrius-pseudo:
Pseudo-Demetrius, or False Demetrius, is the name history gives to three Muscovite pretenders who claimed to be Demetrius, son of Ivan the Terrible. The real Demetrius had been murdered as a child at Uglich in 1591. The first pretender, probably a grandson of the boyar Bogdan Otrepev, won Lithuanian and Polish backing. He entered Moscow in triumph in June 1605, and was crowned tsar that July after Boris Godunov's sudden death.

His reforms, toleration and love of Western ways alarmed the boyars, and Basil Shuisky's conspiracy slew him in the Kremlin in May 1606, days after his wedding to Marina Mniszek. A second pretender, the thief of Tushino, gathered over 100,000 men before his murder in 1610. A third, the thief of Pskov, was executed at Moscow in 1612.
britannica-1911-fanti-manfredo:
Manfredo Fanti, an Italian general born at Carpi in 1806, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was trained at the army school of Modena. In 1831 he joined the revolt led by Ciro Menotti. Sentenced to death and hanged in effigy, he fled to France.

French service gave him work with the corps of engineers. He then fought in Spain for Queen Christina against the Carlists for thirteen years. When war came between Piedmont and Austria in 1848, he hurried home to Italy. He led a Lombard brigade and was picked for the Piedmontese chamber in 1849. Doubt from senior officers shadowed his later path.
britannica-1911-galiani-ferdinando:
Galiani, Ferdinando (1728–1787), an Italian economist, was born at Chieti on the 2nd of December 1728 and educated by his uncle at Naples and Rome for the Church. At twenty-two, in orders, he had written a treatise on money in the mercantile school. A mock volume on the death of the hangman made his name as a wit. In 1759 he became secretary to the Neapolitan embassy at Paris and held the post for ten years.

Back at Naples he rose, becoming minister of the royal domains in 1777. His book, the Dialogues sur le commerce des blés, treated the corn trade with such wit that Voltaire compared its making to Plato and Molière. Its principle was that no system fits all countries in this trade. Galiani shared mercantilist errors, even defending the debasement of currency. He died at Naples on the 30th of October 1787.
britannica-1911-gando:
Gando is a sultanate of British West Africa inside the protectorate of Nigeria, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives its place and past. It sits on the left bank of the Niger above Borgu. The sultanate was set up about 1819, on the death of Othman Dan Fodio, founder of the Fula empire. Its size and weight shifted much during the nineteenth century.

Several Fula emirates counted as its tributaries, while Gando itself leaned more or less on Sokoto. At mid-century it held both banks of the Niger at least as far as Say. The districts outside the British protectorate now belong to France. Gando has been in treaty relations with the British since 1884. In 1903 its British share passed firmly under the Nigerian administration, and its emir was appointed under British authority after the fall of Sokoto.
britannica-1911-gorges-sir-ferdinando:
Sir Ferdinando Gorges, founder of Maine, is followed in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Somerset about 1566, he chose the sword and the sea. At twenty-one a ship of the Spanish Armada took him prisoner. He fought for Henry the Fourth of France and was knighted at Rouen. In 1596 he took charge of the fort and castle at Plymouth.

Gorges sailed with Essex to the Azores and to Ireland. He was caught up in Essex's rising in London as well. Cast out in 1603, he was soon back at his Plymouth post. Pay failed for years and the fort fell to ruin under him. He quit in 1629, but his mind had turned to America. There he drove the planting of the Popham colony in 1607.
britannica-1911-hokkaido: Hokkaido is the Japanese name for the northern division of the empire of Japan. The name itself is built of three parts: Hoku, north; kai, sea; and do, road. That northern division takes in Yezo, the Kuriles and their neighbouring islets. The whole entry is a single short sentence giving the name, its parts and the lands it covers, and nothing more.
britannica-1911-mameli-goffredo:
Mameli, Goffredo is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an Italian poet and patriot who died at twenty one. Mameli was born at Genoa in 1827 to a noble family, was schooled at the Scolopi College and read law and philosophy at Genoa. At nineteen he wrote to Mazzini and gave himself wholly to the cause. In the autumn of 1847 he wrote the song Fratelli d'Italia.

That song rang through every district of Italy in 1848 and 1849. Mameli served in the National Guard at Genoa, fought as a volunteer in Lombardy, and went to Rome when the republic was proclaimed there. When the French army closed on the city he joined the ranks and won the esteem of Garibaldi. Wounded in April, he fought on, was hit worse in June, and died in hospital on the sixth of July 1849.
britannica-1911-marsigli-luigi-ferdinand:
Luigi Ferdinando Marsigli was an Italian soldier and man of science who lived from sixteen fifty-eight to seventeen thirty. He was born at Bologna and learned science in his home town. He then roamed Turkey to note its host and its wild life. On his return he joined the hosts of the chief ruler.

He fought the Turks, was hurt and seized, and was sold to a lord whom he went with to the siege of Vienna. Freed by a fee, he fought on, then lost his rank by a courts blame. He spent his last years on sea study. His stores of finds formed the core of a new hall at Bologna.
britannica-1911-mikado:
Mikado is the poetic title that foreign lands link with the ruler of Japan, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The word is Japanese for exalted gate. The home title that means emperor is tenno. A second term is used for his role in dealings abroad.

Under the charter of eighteen eighty nine, the emperor gave much of his old full power to the people's chosen men. As head of the empire he still names ministers. He declares war, makes peace, and seals treaties. From sixteen hundred to eighteen sixty eight, real power lay with the shoguns. They still took their post, in form, from the mikado. The revolt of eighteen sixty seven gave real power back.
britannica-1911-mondonedo:
Mondonedo is a city of northern Spain, in the province of Lugo, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes the place and its past. It stands in a sheltered valley on the river Masma, twenty-seven miles north of Lugo, with 10,590 people in 1900. The northern spurs of the Cantabrian Mountains ring the valley.

The entry names the cathedral, a Corinthian building of the seventeenth century, a former Franciscan convent now used as a theatre and school, and the civil hospital. Lace-making, linen-weaving, and leather work are its trades. By local tradition its bishopric came from Dumium in the eighth century, and the city was retaken from the Moors in 858.
britannica-1911-paer-ferdinando:
Ferdinando Paer is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Parma on the first of June 1771, he was an Italian writer of operas. He learned the craft of music from a violin player who had trained at Naples. His first opera came out when he was only sixteen.

The article follows a career across the courts of Europe. Fresh operas made his name known all through Italy. Posts at Vienna and Dresden followed, with a life post as court music chief in 1804. Napoleon took a shine to him in 1807 and carried him to Warsaw and Paris. There he led the Italian opera house for some years. He wrote forty three operas in all, in the style of older Italian masters. The text rates his work as light in weight, loved in his day and soon forgot.
britannica-1911-palacio-valdes-armando:
Armando Palacio Valdes (1853-) is a Spanish writer of tales and criticism. He was born at Entralgo in Asturias on 4 October 1853. His first pieces were sharp essays printed in the Revista Europea. They showed free judgment and fine humour, and won such favour that he was soon made editor of that journal. His best critical work is gathered in books of 1878 and 1882.

In 1881 Palacio Valdes brought out a novel, El Senorito Octavio. It showed a rare power to watch and note life, and the promise of more to come. Marta y Maria of 1883 tells of a clash between a call to the religious life and earthly love. That book won a broad triumph and set him in the first rank of Spanish novelists of his day. El Idilio de un enfermo of 1884 is in large part the tale of his own life.
britannica-1911-pasquini-bernardo:
Bernardo Pasquini (1637-1710), an Italian composer, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Massa in Tuscany in December 1637. He was a pupil of two teachers from the age of thirteen. He came to Rome while still young and entered the service of Prince Borghese. Later he became organist of a great church there.

He enjoyed the shelter of Queen Christina of Sweden, in whose honour an opera of his was staged in 1679. During the second stay of Alessandro Scarlatti in Rome, Pasquini and Corelli often performed with him. All three belonged to the Arcadian Academy. He died at Rome in November 1710 and was buried in a church there. The entry says he deserves to be remembered as a strong composer for the harpsichord, and points to a book on the piano sonata for an account of that music.
britannica-1911-phaedo:
Phaedo was a Greek philosopher who founded the Elian school, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells. He was a native of Elis, born in the last years of the fifth century before Christ. In the war of 401 to 400 between Sparta and Elis he was taken and made a slave in Athens. His beauty brought him a sad fame there.

He became a pupil of Socrates, who held him in warm love. He was close to Cebes and to Plato, and he gave his name to one of the dialogues of Plato. One old tale says he flatly denied that he held the views Plato lays on him. After the death of Socrates he went home to Elis, where his pupils held his school. Later men moved the school to Eretria. His own doctrines are not known, and none of his dialogues, all lost, can be read now.
britannica-1911-piatti-carlo-alfredo:
Carlo Alfredo Piatti is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an Italian master of the cello born at Bergamo in eighteen twenty two. His father played the violin, and the boy was schooled at Milan. From his late teens he toured the great towns of Europe in triumph.

The entry tells how London crowds took him to their hearts at once. For close to forty years he led the cello desk at famed chamber shows. Pure style, wide taste, and charm marked the man beyond his skill. A feast marked fifty years since his first London stage night. Ill health drove him from public life in his last four years.
britannica-1911-rio-pardo:
Rio Pardo is a town of Brazil in its far south state, set on the left bank of a river at the point where a second stream joins it. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the wide area of its district and two counts of its folk, for the whole district and for the town alone. Rail and boat link it to the state port city.

Small boats can steam up the river to the town, the entry says. It was once a key post for troops and a hub of trade. The spread of rail lines has cut that role back much. The lands round it are rich but thinly tilled, and the raise of stock is its chief work. Its root was a border fort built by the Portuguese, and it rose to town rank in time.
britannica-1911-rondo:
Rondo is a form in music that grew out of a form in verse, explains a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Early cases show up in songs by Orlando di Lasso. French harpsichord works by Couperin and his peers show the same link in name and shape.

In the old form, one neat phrase returns again and again. Short parts that differ a bit sit between each return. Bach made the form richer but did not widen its range. In later use, the term covers a key part of sonata forms, most often in last movements. There the main tune is broad, and the parts between returns sit in other keys and stand in sharp contrast.
britannica-1911-sado:
Sado, an island of Japan, is set out in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The island lies west of Niigata in the sea off the main coast. It runs to about one hundred and thirty miles round. Its area is given as three hundred and thirty-six square miles. About one hundred and thirteen thousand people lived there at the time.

The port of Ebisa stands on the east coast of the island. Near the west coast sits Aikawa, a town by gold and silver mines. Those mines made Sado famed and were worked from early times. Two hill ranges run side by side, split by a low neck of land. The high peak of Kimpokuzan tops the north range.
britannica-1911-san-fernando:
San Fernando, a seaport of southern Spain in the province of Cadiz, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands on the Isla de León, a rocky island among salt marshes on Cadiz Bay. Its people numbered 29,635 in 1900. With Ferrol and Cartagena, it is one of the three chief naval ports of Spain. Each port is governed by an admiral with the title of captain-general.

A railway links the town with Cadiz, and a tram runs from the arsenal at La Carraca. The main buildings serve the navy: workshops, barracks, an academy, an observatory, and a hospital. Salt is made nearby and stone is quarried. Local making includes spirits, leather, soap, hats, sails, and ropes, plus a large iron foundry. The town was likely a Carthaginian settlement. Its arsenal dates from 1790, and the Cortes met there in 1810. The present name dates only from 1813.
britannica-1911-teredo:
Teredo is a genus of molluscs best known as the ship worms. The 1911 Britannica entry places them in the lamellibranch class of shellfish. They are famed for the ruin they cause in ships' timbers at sea. Harbour woodwork, piles, and all wood long sunk in salt water suffer. They bore long round holes deep into the wood they infest.

The worms crowd thick in those holes, with scant wood left between. Each bore is lined with a chalky layer the mollusc secretes. That lining stops short of the deep end where boring goes on. Bores run most oft with the grain of the wood they eat. When a bore is sealed at full length, the tube ends round.
britannica-1911-tornado:
Tornado is a wild local whirlwind treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Spanish word for a turning about. A tornado most often forms in a thunderstorm. In look it is a funnel of cloud that hangs from the storm cloud above. When full grown it thins down to the earth at its point.

With its whirl it has a march of its own, at twenty to forty miles an hour. On its narrow track it leaves ruin. Its life is most often from half an hour to an hour. Tornadoes are most common in America, in the Mississippi Valley and the southern states, and rare in Europe. They go with storms and so come in warm weather. The cause, the article says, is a patch of unsteady air high above the earth.
britannica-1911-trinidad-colorado:
Trinidad is a city in southern Colorado and the seat of Las Animas county. The 1911 Britannica article puts it about one hundred miles south of Pueblo. Its count rose from 5,345 in 1900 to 10,204 in 1910. Four rail lines serve the town, plus small electric lines to coal towns near by. The streets lie on a hilly site on both banks of the Purgatory river. Raton Peak rises ten miles to the south.

The entry lists a Carnegie library, a federal building, an opera house, and a park. The town sits in a coal and coke district with much stock raising. Farms near by grow alfalfa, beans, and sugar beets, much of the land by ditch water. Town works include rail shops, foundries, coke ovens, and a wool cleaning mill.
britannica-1911-tuxedo:
Tuxedo, a town in Orange County, New York, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands about forty miles north-west of New York City, near the New Jersey line. The census of 1910 counted 2,858 people there. The Erie railway served the town.

West of the station lies Tuxedo Lake, ringed by some thirteen thousand acres of land. The elder Pierre Lorillard took the tract for a debt in 1814 and built a shooting box there. His grandson formed the Tuxedo Park Association to develop the ground. The Tuxedo Club and Tuxedo Park opened in June 1886. A set of wealthy families built country houses inside the park as a closed social club. The grounds held golf links, tennis courts, game preserves, and fine trout and bass fishing.
britannica-1911-vinci-leonardo:
Leonardo Vinci, who lived from 1690 to 1730, was an Italian opera composer. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica separates his comic and serious fame. He was born at Strongoli in Calabria in 1690. He trained at a Naples school for poor boys under a noted master.

Comic operas in Naples dialect first made Vinci name in 1719. One such work from 1722 still ranks as his best there. His serious operas show a cut and force of drama. Burney praised that direct power in print, the entry notes. Two Rome works of 1728 and 1730 lead that side of his output. A famed air from the second shows his style at its height. He died by poison in 1730, the entry states plainly.
canyons-of-the-colorado:
J. W. Powell wrote the tale of his Colorado River runs, first printed in 1895. Powell had run the United States Geological Survey. Rich plates fill the book. A wry preface opens it: home from the first run, he found the papers full of his death.

All hands lost save one, the news had held. A friend had kept the death notes in a pile. In false death he found a fame his life has not kept, Powell jokes. Science, not sport, drove the run, he owns in plain words: land and rock were its aims. Falls, rapids, and sheer walls fill the tale the preface frames. First-hand sight of a land no white man had mapped gives the book its weight to this day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonso-tostad:
Alonso Tostado, or Tostatus, was an exegete, born at Madrigal about 1400, dead near Avila in 1455. After Franciscan grammar school he entered Salamanca, studying philosophy, theology, law, Greek, and Hebrew. By application, brilliance, and a retentive memory, his learning made contemporaries call him the wonder of the world. Aged twenty-two, he lectured on many subjects to large audiences and later assisted with distinction at Basle.

While visiting the papal court at Siena in 1443, Eugene IV received a denunciation of him for heretical propositions, but assured the pontiff of his orthodoxy by letter. In his Defensorium against Torquemada and critics, he opposed the pope's authority. Back in Spain, he rose to Chancellor of Castile, then Bishop of Avila in 1449, source of his title Abulensis. Besides a Spanish Eusebius commentary, he wrote on Old Testament histories to Second Paralipomenon and on Matthew's Gospel. These digressions appeared at Venice in thirteen folio volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonzo-de-alv:
Alonzo de Alvarado, Knight of Santiago, born at Secadura de Trasmiera near Burgos, date unknown, died in 1559. He went to Peru with Pedro de Alvarado in 1534, no relative of the latter. Charged by contemporaries with avarice and cruelty, he was unflinching for Spain through Peru's civil wars from about 1537 to 1555. He always sided with the crown's sincere representatives, not always profitably. In the bloody troubles that followed he served as a prominent leader, always unsuccessful in immediate command.

Still, a mainstay of the Spanish cause, he held high position. When Hernández Girón rebelled in 1553, Alvarado commanded against him, but at Chuquinga in 1554 suffered a signal defeat. Melancholy after that disaster, he wasted away and died five years later. His chief achievement, pacifying Chachapoyas in northeastern Peru in 1535 and 1536, was the first step from Peru towards the Amazon basin. He married in Spain on a short visit in 1544.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-de-al:
Quito-born soldier Antonio de Alcedo lived from 1755 into the early nineteenth century. He rose to brigadier general in the Spanish army and wrote a five-volume historical and geographical dictionary of the West Indies. His father had presided over the Royal Audiencia, the high court and governing body, at Quito. Alcedo built his dictionary on a 1771 Italian work by the Jesuit Giovanni Coletti on South America, expanding it into a reference for the Spanish Indies.

An English version by G. A. Thompson appeared in 1812, and many readers took it for an improvement. The article warns that the translation in fact teems with errors largely absent from the original. Readers get a short life of a soldier-scholar, plus a caution about trusting a translated reference work over the Spanish text it claims to render.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-ignacio-de: Blessed Ignacio de Azevedo, a Jesuit missionary, was born at Oporto in 1528 and martyred near Palma in the Canary Islands in 1570. He joined the Jesuits at Coimbra in 1548, served as rector at Lisbon, provincial of Portugal, and visitor of the Brazil missions. Returning to Brazil with thirty-nine companions, he was seized and killed by Huguenot pirates, dying with his band for the faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caspar-hurtad:
Caspar Hurtado was a Spanish Jesuit and theologian born at Mondejar in New Castile in 1575 who died at Alcalá in August 1647. At Alcalá University he won first place in the doctorate examination against many rivals and became professor at once, winning fame as a lecturer. At thirty-two he gave up his chair to enter the Society of Jesus in 1607, then lectured in theology at Murcia, Madrid, and Alcalá.

He died as dean of the Alcalá faculty, where he had taught for thirty years. His works cover the Eucharist, marriage and censures, the Incarnation, the sacraments, beatitude and human acts, and God. Among Jesuits he ranks high for learning and piety. He broke early from Thomas Aquinas's method, which most theologians then followed, to build a system of his own. His exposition won praise for brevity, clarity, and conciseness, and he preached with great success at court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colorado:
Robert Morrison's entry covers Colorado, the thirty-fifth state admitted to the Union. It lies between the 37th and 41st parallels and the 102nd and 109th meridians. Its straight borders form a parallelogram, set across the Rocky Mountains. Colonel William Gilpin, its first governor, argued that railroads and unity had replaced natural bounds. After the Cliff-dwellers came the Utes and Arapahoes. French and Spanish claims gave way to the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, the Texas cession of 1850, and the cession from Mexico.

Morrison moves from land to people: plains in the east, a dry and healthful climate, and 539,700 people by the 1900 census. Mining and farming led its industries, with wheat near twenty-one bushels an acre. Public schools served the whole state, with a university at Boulder. History runs from Coronado in 1541 through Civil War loyalty to woman suffrage, adopted by vote in 1893. Church notes close the survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denver-colora:
A diocesan history of Denver, a suffragan of Santa Fé erected in 1887 across the whole state of Colorado. A Spanish colony from New Mexico settled on the Conejos River in 1852 and built the first church in 1858. Gold found near Denver the same year drew crowds eastward, and mining towns spread through the Pike's Peak country.

Bishop Miège of Leavenworth visited Denver in 1860, then had the distant missions moved to Santa Fé's care. Joseph Machebeuf and John Raverdy arrived that October and laboured almost alone for over seven years, raising churches across a vast field. Later pages note Italian, Slav, and Spanish tongues in use, and record a diocese free of debt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-collado:
Diego Collado was a Spanish Dominican born late in the sixteenth century at Miajadas. He reached Japan in 1619 while Christians there faced harsh persecution. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him to Rome and Spain after the martyrdom of a fellow friar. There he won concessions for the missions of the East despite the ill will of rivals.

He returned to Asia in 1635 with papal and royal letters. He tried and failed to found a Philippines convent given wholly to the Chinese and Japanese missions. Recalled to Spain, he died in a shipwreck in 1638, staying aboard to hear confessions and prepare his fellow voyagers for death. His Japanese grammar and Chinese dictionary crown the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-lopez-d:
Diego Lopez de Cogolludo ranks among the chief historians of Yucatan. His History of Yucatan was printed at Madrid in 1688 and reprinted twice in the nineteenth century. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry values the book because Cogolludo gathered facts in person. Older written and spoken sources, now partly vanished, could still be consulted in his day.

He drew heavily on Bishop Diego de Landa, the entry warns, so his statements call for careful checking. Born at Alcala de Henares, he took the Franciscan habit in 1629 and crossed to Yucatan. There he rose to lector in theology, guardian, and at last provincial of his order in the province he chronicled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flavio-biondo:
Flavio Biondo was an Italian archaeologist and historian born at Forli in 1388. He founded the study of archaeology and of Christian and medieval topography. At Milan he found the only manuscript of Cicero's dialogue Brutus and copied it. From 1432 he served as secretary to Eugenius IV, then to Nicholas V, Calixtus III, and Pius II.

His three encyclopedias became the basis of all later dictionaries of Roman antiquities. Roma Instaurata described Rome's monuments and churches; Roma Triumphans, Roman customs and institutions. Italia Illustrata mapped Italy in fourteen regions, listing its cities. His great history ran from the fall of Rome to 1440, but death left it unfinished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fra-giovanni-:
Fra Giovanni Giocondo, born at Verona about 1445 and dead at Venice about 1525, was an Italian architect, antiquary, and classical scholar who moved between the Dominican and Franciscan orders. He taught Latin and Greek at Verona, where the young Scaliger was a pupil. He visited Rome to sketch ancient buildings and explain defaced inscriptions, and in 1492 presented Lorenzo de' Medici with a collection of ancient manuscripts. His learning helped feed the revival of classical studies.

As an architect he designed Verona's Palazzo del Consiglio, planned fortifications for Treviso, and advised Venice on protecting its lagoons by diverting the Brenta river to the sea. He also produced the first correct illustrated edition of Vitruvius, printed at Venice in 1511, edited Caesar's Commentaries, and drew Caesar's bridge over the Rhine. His last work was probably rebuilding Verona's bridge in 1521.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-tor:
Francesco Torbido, often called Il Moro, the Moor, was a Veronese painter and engraver. He was born at Verona about 1486 and still living in 1546, when a letter of Aretino mentions him. He studied at Venice under Giorgione, returned to Verona, married a daughter of Count Zenovello Giusti, and became pupil and adopted heir of Liberale. He stayed at Verona, painting portraits and frescoes in churches and on house fronts, as was the Veronese fashion of the day.

His work blends the influences of his Venetian master and of Veronese artists into a style of his own, keeping the rich, glowing colour he learned from Giorgione. Fine frescoes survive at Verona cathedral, a Nativity and Assumption signed and dated 1534, and at San Fermo, Sant' Eufemia, and San Zeno. His portraits can be studied at Naples, Venice, and the Brera. Two portraits show the artist himself, one at Munich dated 1516.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-mac:
Francisco Macedo, known as a Sancto Augustino, was a theologian born at Coimbra in Portugal in 1596 and dead at Padua on 1 May 1681. He was a man of enormous erudition and restless change. He entered the Jesuits in 1610, left them in 1638 for the Discalced Franciscans, left those in 1648 for the Observants, and sided in Portugal with the House of Braganza. Called to Rome by Alexander VII, he taught theology at the Propaganda, church history at the Sapienza, and served as consultor to the Inquisition.

At Venice in 1667, during the week from 26 September, he staged a public disputation against all comers on almost every branch of knowledge, Bible, theology, patrology, history, law, literature, and poetry. He named it in quaint style the literary roar of the Lion of St. Mark. It won him the freedom of Venice and the moral philosophy chair at Padua.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-tol:
Francisco Toledo, son of an actuary, was born at Cordova on 4 October 1532 and died at Rome on 14 September 1596, a Jesuit philosopher, theologian, exegete, and cardinal. He studied philosophy at Valencia and theology with Domingo Soto at Salamanca, taught philosophy there at twenty-three, and after ordination entered the Society of Jesus in 1558. At Rome from 1559 he served as master of novices, professor of philosophy and of scholastic and moral theology, and prefect of studies at the Roman College.

He was theologian of the Sacred Penitentiary and preacher to pope and cardinals for twenty-four years. He accompanied missions to Emperor Maximilian and King Sigismund of Poland, served as envoy to Vienna, Poland, Germany, Bavaria, and Louvain. There he received Baius's abjuration of condemned propositions, and was made cardinal by Clement VIII in 1593. Mariana judged him of ordinary virtue, yet his commentaries on Aristotle and Thomas endured.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-vas:
Francisco Vasquez de Coronado, born at Salamanca in 1510 and dead in Mexico in 1553, was the Spanish explorer of the American Southwest. He reached Mexico before 1538 and won the favour of Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza, who made him governor of New Galicia in 1538. In 1539 the viceroy sent Father Marcos de Niza with Estevanico to scout northward on reports from Cabeza de Vaca. When Marcos returned with tales of settled Indians beyond Mexico, Mendoza ordered an expedition and made Coronado its commander.

 Gathering at Compostela with about 300 Spaniards, 1000 Indians, 1000 horses, and six small cannon. With sheep and cattle for colonising, Coronado spent two years visiting almost every inhabited pueblo of New Mexico. He began with Zuni, the Seven Cities of Cibola of Marcos's report, and pushed on across plains that yielded no gold, ending his great march in disappointment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fray-francisc:
Francisco de Alvarado, a Dominican born in Mexico, is remembered for a single book on a language of Oaxaca. He entered his order in July 1574 and later served as vicar of Tamazulapa, but almost nothing else about his life survives. The Catholic Encyclopedia entry rests on the one work that keeps his name alive.

At Mexico in 1593 he published a vocabulary of Mixtec, one of the tongues spoken in what is now the state of Oaxaca. In that same year and city, a fellow Dominican named Antonio de los Reyes brought out a grammar of the same language. Because the two books appeared together, no one can say which of them deserves credit as the first work on Mixtec.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacopo-belgr:
Giacopo Belgrado was an Italian Jesuit and natural philosopher, born at Udine in 1704 and dead there in 1789. Of a noble family, he studied at Padua, entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1723, and learned mathematics and philosophy at Bologna. He taught letters at Venice, then theology at Parma, where he became professor of mathematics and physics for twelve years. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his rise from teacher to court scholar.

At Parma he ran physics experiments with apparatus built by two assistants, and in 1757 he raised an observatory on a tower of the college. He served as confessor first to the Duchess and then to Duke Don Philippo, who also named him court mathematician. In 1773 he became rector of the college at Bologna. His books ranged from electric phenomena and the feel of cold and heat to the screw of Archimedes and proofs of God's existence drawn from geometry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girolamo-seri:
Girolamo Seripando was an Italian theologian and cardinal born at Troja in Apulia in 1493, who died at Trent in 1563. Intended for law, he entered the Augustinian Order at Viterbo at fourteen, adding Greek and Hebrew to philosophy and theology. He lectured at Siena in 1515, taught theology at Bologna in 1517, and became vicar-general in 1532. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows an elegant and prolific writer.

Elected superior general in 1539, he governed twelve years with prudence, zeal, and piety, and won such fame as a preacher that Charles V often attended his sermons. At the Council of Trent in 1546 he pressed for purity of the scriptural text and held peculiar views on original sin and justification. Made cardinal in 1561, he became first president of the council after Cardinal Gonzaga's death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-toal:
Giuseppe Toaldo was a priest and physicist born at Pianezze in 1719, who died at Padua in 1797. He entered the Padua seminary at fourteen, later taught mathematics and Italian literature there, and edited the works of Galileo in 1744. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a champion of the lightning-rod against popular prejudice.

Made pastor of Montegalda in 1754, he was called to the chair of astronomy at Padua eight years later. With fellow priests Divisch and Beccaria he studied atmospheric electricity and protection against lightning. He adopted Franklin's views over the French school of Abbé Nollet. His treatises of 1772 and 1774 helped place conductors on the Siena Cathedral, the tower of Saint Mark's in Venice, powder magazines, and Venetian naval ships.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignacio-barbo:
Ignacio Barbosa Machado was a Portuguese historian, born at Lisbon in 1686 and dead in 1734. Coimbra University educated him; Brazil then received him as a magistrate, and after his wife's death he entered the clerical state. He left several historical works, chief among them his Fastos Politicos e Militares de Antiqua e Nova Lusitania, published at Lisbon in 1745, on Portugal's and Brazil's history.

He was brother to the more famous Diego Barbosa Machado, also priest and writer. Diego authored the Bibliotheca Lusitana, Historica, Critica e Chronologica, published from 1741 to 1759, a notable monument of Portuguese literature. Ignacio's own work, though shorter-lived than his brother's, stands as a solid contribution to Luso-Brazilian history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-de-pra:
Jerome de Prado, a Spanish Jesuit exegete born at Baeza in 1547 and dead at Rome in 1595. He entered the Society in 1572, taught literature, and held the Scripture chair at Córdoba for sixteen years. His life's work was a commentary on Ezekiel.

After sixteen years Prado had reached only chapter twenty-six when he died at Rome seeking illustrations. His fellow Jesuit Villalpando finished the task in two more volumes, with a detailed study of the Temple and an apparatus on Jerusalem's city and temple. The set, praised for Jewish coins, weights, and measures, was paid for at Philip II's request. Prado also left notes on Isaiah, Zechariah, and Hebrews.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-marie-:
Joseph-Marie de Gérando was a French statesman and writer who gave his talents to education and charity. Born at Lyons in 1772, he defended the city against the Convention's armies, was wounded and captured, and escaped to Switzerland and Naples. A prize essay on signs and the formation of ideas, written at Colmar, changed his life.

Called to Paris, Gérando served on the Council of State under Napoleon and Louis XVIII and helped found the Society for Elementary Instruction in 1815, bringing England's monitorial system to France's poor. He opened a law course in 1819, entered the Chamber of Peers in 1837, and founded schools, hospitals, and charities. He died at Paris in 1842.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-bautista:
Juan Bautista de Toledo was the Spanish architect who planned the Escorial. Born at Madrid at an unknown date, he went to Rome in 1547 and studied under Michelangelo's influence. Sent to Naples by the viceroy, he designed streets, churches, bastions, and fountains there as architect to Emperor Charles V.

Called home by Philip II in 1559, Toledo became architect-in-chief of the royal works in Spain. At Madrid his designs included the Casa de la Misericordia and works at Aranjuez, then drew the plan for the Escorial and saw its first stone laid on 23 April 1563. He directed the building until his death in 1567.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-queve:
Juan de Quevedo was the first bishop appointed for mainland America. A Franciscan from Old Castile whose early life is unknown, he was named Bishop of Santa Maria de la Antigua, or Darien, by Pope Leo X. The appointment came on 28 August 1513 at King Ferdinand's request. He sailed with Governor Pedrarias in April 1514 and landed that June.

Quevedo watched the governor's men commit cruelties against Indians and rivals, including the beheading of Balboa, discoverer of the Pacific. Las Casas charged him with wealth-seeking and neglect, charges the entry calls uncertain. Back in Spain in 1518, Quevedo urged Charles to curb governors' powers and protect natives, then died at Barcelona in 1519.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-maldonad:
Juan Maldonado was a Spanish Jesuit theologian and Bible scholar of the Counter-Reformation. Born in 1533 at Casas de Reina, he studied at Salamanca under Soto and other masters, taught philosophy, theology, and Greek, and joined the Society of Jesus in 1562. Sent to Paris, he lectured at the Collège de Clermont from 1564.

Maldonado preached missions in Calvinist Poitou, won converts among Protestant princes, and disputed with Calvinist preachers before the Duchess of Bouillon at Sedan. His lectures on theology and Scripture drew crowds, and his commentaries became standard tools for Catholic preachers. Ill health cut his Paris years short, and he died at Rome in 1583.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luiz-de-azeve:
Luiz de Azevedo was a Jesuit missionary and scholar in Ethiopia, born in Portugal in 1573 and dead in Ethiopia in 1634. He joined the Society in 1588, sailed for the Indies in 1592, and laboured in Ethiopia from 1605 until his death.

Called the Apostle Agarus, he ranks among the most illustrious doctors of Ethiopia's church, winning many schismatics back to Catholicism. He put Toletus on Romans and Ribera on Hebrews into Chaldaic, with the Canonical Hours and the Office of Our Lady. He wrote a grammar of Ethiopic, and rendered the New Testament, a Portuguese catechism, and creed instructions into the same tongue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mageddo:
